--- title: "Formatting Values" guide-section: "Using tinytab" bread-crumbs: false --- tinytab has three functions for turning a single number into a display string. They share the same rules: the value is the first argument, and every option is a keyword argument. ## Numbers [`fmt_number()`](../reference/fmt_number.qmd) rounds to a fixed number of decimal places (2 by default) and groups thousands with a separator: ::: {#f71e92ce .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from tinytab import fmt_number fmt_number(1234567.891) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` '1,234,567.89' ``` ::: ::: Use `decimals=` to change the precision: ::: {#e3eefa0a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} fmt_number(1234567.891, decimals=0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` '1,234,568' ``` ::: ::: The thousands separator is a comma by default. Set another with `sep_mark=`: ::: {#8adc2f20 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} fmt_number(1234567.891, sep_mark=" ") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` '1 234 567.89' ``` ::: ::: ## Percentages [`fmt_percent()`](../reference/fmt_percent.qmd) takes a proportion, where `1` means 100%, and shows one decimal place by default: ::: {#cde3c44f .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} from tinytab import fmt_percent fmt_percent(0.256) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` '25.6%' ``` ::: ::: ::: {#4907f39e .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} fmt_percent(0.256, decimals=0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` '26%' ``` ::: ::: ## Currencies [`fmt_currency()`](../reference/fmt_currency.qmd) adds a currency symbol and uses the right number of decimal places for the currency. US dollars are the default: ::: {#f9ce7dc4 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} from tinytab import fmt_currency fmt_currency(1234.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` '$1,234.50' ``` ::: ::: Choose another currency with a three-letter code (in any case). Yen are shown without decimal places, and negative amounts put the sign before the symbol: ::: {#e6acc01d .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} [ fmt_currency(1234.5, currency="eur"), fmt_currency(1234.5, currency="JPY"), fmt_currency(-5, currency="GBP"), ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` ['€1,234.50', '¥1,234', '-£5.00'] ``` ::: ::: The supported codes are USD, EUR, GBP, and JPY. Any other code is an error, and the message lists the valid ones: ::: {#0ba453f5 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} fmt_currency(10, currency="XYZ") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: ## Only numbers All three functions accept only numbers (integers and floats). Anything else, including a number written as a string, raises a `TypeError`: ::: {#b7cebf39 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} fmt_number("10") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: `True` and `False` are rejected too, even though Python treats them as the integers 1 and 0. Formatting a boolean as "1.00" is almost always a mistake.
